name: Apache TsFile
summary: A columnar file format for device time series, with per-series indexes and time-series encodings; the storage format of Apache IoTDB and its own Apache project since 2023.
intro: A TsFile holds the readings of many devices, organised in four layers. A page stores a run of one series’ timestamps and values in time order, as two separate columns. A chunk is a header plus pages for one series. A chunk group holds the chunks of one device written in the same period. An index at the end of the file locates each series’ chunks and keeps file-level statistics. Minimum and maximum time and value and the count of points are kept for the file, each chunk and each page, so a reader skips pages that can’t match and answers some aggregates without decoding data. Unlike Parquet or ORC, metadata is stored per series, so reading one series never touches the metadata of the others.

Each column is encoded for its shape and then compressed: `TS_2DIFF` (second-order differences) for timestamps and counters, `GORILLA` or `CHIMP` for floats that change slowly, `DICTIONARY` for repetitive strings, `RLE`, `SPRINTZ`, `RLBE` and others, followed by LZ4 by default, or Snappy, ZSTD, GZIP or LZMA2. Since 2.0 (January 2025) the format also has a table model that matches IoTDB’s: a table per device type, string `TAG` columns that together identify a device, `FIELD` columns for the measurements, and a time column that must be in order for each device.

Libraries exist for Java, C++, C and Python (`pip install tsfile`), and the Python package can open a folder of TsFiles as a lazy, DataFrame-like view. DuckDB reads and writes table-model TsFiles through a community extension. IoTDB loads a TsFile with one `LOAD` statement or by watching a folder, so an edge device can write files offline and ship them later. TsFile grew inside IoTDB at Tsinghua University and became a top-level Apache project on 15 November 2023, without passing through the Incubator. The latest release is 2.4.0 (July 2026); a 1.1.x line is kept for IoTDB 1.x.
strengths: Per-series indexes and statistics at file, chunk and page level, so a query for one device and time range reads only the chunks it needs
Encodings built for sensor data (second-order deltas, Gorilla, Chimp, Sprintz), chosen per column
The same files are IoTDB’s storage, so data written on a device or in Python loads straight into the database without conversion
Apache 2.0, with native libraries for Java, C++, C and Python, a DuckDB extension, and bundled scripts that convert CSV, Parquet and Arrow files
limits: Few engines read it compared with Parquet: outside IoTDB there’s the DuckDB extension (local, table-model files only) and a Spark connector documented only for Spark 2.4.3
The Python guide covers only the table model, and `TsFileDataFrame` reads only numeric fields, skipping `STRING`, `TEXT`, `BLOB` and `DATE` columns
`RLE` and `TS_2DIFF` keep only two decimal places of a float by default; `GORILLA` is the recommended lossless choice
Rows must arrive in time order per device (DuckDB’s writer wants them sorted by tag columns, then time), and the 1.1.x and 2.x lines pair with different IoTDB major versions

story: TsFile was born inside IoTDB at Tsinghua University. When the team proposed IoTDB to the Apache Incubator in 2018, TsFile was the part already open source on GitHub, described as a columnar format similar to Parquet and CarbonData but built for time series of the form device, series, timestamp, value.

Its design started from how sensors behave. Two sensors on one device rarely sample at the same millisecond, so forcing them into rows means storing nulls, and Parquet’s repetition and definition levels for nested data add work that flat series don’t need. TsFile stores each series with its own timestamps, puts time-series statistics in every page header, and keeps a device’s chunk groups in time order so a time-range scan can stop early. IoTDB used it as its storage format, and Hadoop, Hive and Spark could read the same files directly, so analysts didn’t need an export.

In October 2023 the IoTDB community discussed splitting TsFile off so it could serve as a general file format for IoT rather than a database internal. On 15 November 2023 the ASF board established Apache TsFile directly as a top-level project, with an initial PMC of IoTDB committers, and handed it the IoTDB TsFile subproject. Version 1.0.0 followed in February 2024, and 2.0.0 in January 2025 added a format version for the table model. Later releases built out the C++ and Python libraries.

choices.why: Sensors on one device sample at slightly different times. Giving every column chunk its own timestamps avoids padding with nulls and the repetition and definition fields Parquet needs.
Minimum and maximum values and timestamps let a reader skip pages that can’t match a filter, which is most of them in a narrow time-range query.

choices.choice: Metadata indexed per series at the end of the file
choices.why: A query usually asks for a few series of one device. Keeping each series’ metadata separate means a reader doesn’t load metadata for columns it won’t read.
The IoTDB community argued that a format with its encodings and self-describing files could become a standard for IoT data beyond one database, which needed separate governance and releases.
